source_name: AFUE Final Report
topic: Aerial firefighting effectiveness and data collection for wildfire incidents
summary: This report details the Aerial Firefighting Use and Effectiveness (AFUE) longitudinal study conducted from 2015-2018 across 272 wildfire incidents in 18 states [1]. AFUE's mission is to systematically document the operational utilization and tactical contribution of aerial firefighting resources that deliver water and wildland fire chemicals [2]. The study collected data on aircraft performance and effectiveness [2], including attributes like geography, terrain, fuels, weather, liquids dispensed, fire type, tactics, and ground engagement [3, 4]. The data collection team consisted of qualified firefighters with 10 to 25 years of experience [5]. The AFUE study is intended to facilitate timely updates to agency aviation strategy documents and is consistent with past Quadrennial Fire Reviews recommendations to improve performance measurement [5].

source_name: Forest Fire Report 2022
topic: Forest fire management challenges and solutions, operational coordination, and data exchange
summary: This report, dated April 2023, focuses on the 2022 wildfire season in the state of Brandenburg, Germany [6, 7]. It highlights challenges such as the increasing short-term risk of extreme vegetation fires globally, forecasted to rise by a factor of 1.08 to 1.14 within the current decade [8]. The report also notes that qualified data sets on vegetation fires in Brandenburg are currently limited to fires damaging forest areas, excluding those in grain fields and other unpopulated open areas [9]. Proposed solutions include examining technological alternatives to direct firefighting on UXO-contaminated areas, with a focus on unmanned systems to rule out personal injury [10]. More than half of all forest fire reports in 2022 were at danger levels 4 and 5, accounting for 98% (1,380 ha) of the total seasonal damage area [11].

filename: Adapted forest and fire management in climate change – Forest fire climate resilience.pdf
source_name: Forest Fire Climate Resilience
topic: Adapted forest and fire management in climate change, focusing on resilience, prevention, and response
summary: This report details the 'Adapted forest and fire management in climate change – Forest fire climate resilience' (WKR) project, supported by the German Bundestag from May 2020 to January 2024 [12]. The project aims to strengthen the resilience of forests and their managers to climate change and the increasing risk of forest fires in Central Europe, including Germany [13, 14]. Key activities include developing and implementing early wildfire detection systems, including remote sensing [15], and creating training modules for fire departments and forestry professionals, covering topics like fire behavior and firefighting tactics [16-18]. The project has also focused on specialized challenges such as fire management in munitions-contaminated areas, which led to technology procurement in Brandenburg [19-21]. The WKR project also worked on developing a general forest fire strategy [22], improving knowledge exchange, and providing political support for integrated fire management policies [23]. It has engaged with numerous German stakeholders and conducted extensive media work to raise awareness [20, 24-31].

source_name: Canadian Wildland Fire Strategy: A 10-year review and renewed call to action
topic: Canadian wildland fire strategy and review
summary: This document presents the Canadian Wildland Fire Strategy, a 10-year review, and a renewed call to action, available through the Canadian Forest Service Publications website [32]. It is also published in French [32]. The information within the publication can be reproduced for personal or public non-commercial purposes, provided due diligence is exercised in ensuring accuracy, the complete title and author organization are indicated, and it's stated that the reproduction is a copy of an official work published by Natural Resources Canada without affiliation or endorsement [33].

source_name: DFV-FE Vegetation Fire 2020
topic: Vegetation fire expert recommendations and guidelines for firefighting
summary: This document is an expert recommendation from the Forest Fire Working Group in the German Fire Brigade Association, coordinated with the Technical Committee on Operations, Extinguishing Resources, and Environmental Protection [34]. It provides guidelines for fire brigades on using their equipment within their conditions and determining operational resources [35]. The recommendations also cover cooperation between fire brigades and aircraft operators [34], and draw on literature related to fighting forest, moor, and heath fires [35, 36]. It also refers to guidelines for forest fire prevention from Bavarian State Ministries [37].

source_name: The South Canyon Fire Behavior Report
topic: Analysis of fire behavior in the South Canyon Fire incident
summary: This report, published in September 1998, provides a thorough account of the fire behavior during the South Canyon Fire, which was ignited by a lightning strike on July 2, 1994, approximately 7 miles west of Glenwood Springs, Colorado [38, 39]. It summarizes critical factors influencing the fire behavior and the fire environment [38]. The report acknowledges the sacrifice of 14 firefighters who died during the incident and aims to provide information to help prevent future accidents [40, 41]. It describes four separate firefighter groups by their general location during the incident to help readers follow the chain of events [42].

source_name: Fire Management Today Volume 63, No. 3, Summer 2003
topic: Wildland fire behavior case studies and analyses, and firefighter safety
summary: This issue of Fire Management Today, published in Summer 2003, is dedicated to Paul M. Gleason for his contributions to wildland firefighter safety and fire behavior [43]. It is the first part of a special issue on wildland fire behavior case studies and analyses, reprinting past articles to support organizational learning [44]. The articles discuss the value, approaches, and practical uses of such studies [45], emphasizing that wildfires can serve as a source of data for quantitative fire behavior prediction, especially for extreme fire intensity where experimental fires are difficult to arrange [44]. It also includes historical perspectives on fires like the Blackwater Fire [45] and the McVey Fire [46], highlighting the inadequacy of existing firefighting methods for all fire types and the need to understand complex fire behavior [47].

source_name: Fire Management Today Volume 63, No. 4, Fall 2003
topic: Wildland fire behavior case studies, data collection, and reporting standards
summary: This Fall 2003 issue of Fire Management Today is the second installment on wildland fire behavior case studies and analyses, providing examples, methods, reporting standards, and practical advice [48, 49]. It highlights that case studies from one country can be applied to another if fuel type characteristics are relevant, by interpreting burning conditions through their respective fire danger rating systems [49, 50]. The publication notes contributions from U.S. organizations like the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) [51] and Australasian fire researchers [52, 53]. It also provides a suggested outline for preparing a wildland fire behavior case study report, covering introduction, fire environment, analysis, and concluding remarks [54-57]. The report stresses the importance of systematic data collection, particularly recording the position of the head fire at various times [58, 59], and advises on handling information overload and seeking peer review for accuracy [58, 60].

source_name: Fire Documentation
topic: Fire incident documentation and information management
summary: This source discusses aspects of fire documentation and incident management, specifically highlighting experiences in Boden, Sweden [48]. It mentions coordination with rescue teams [49] and the role of an information center in facilitating communication [48]. The report also touches upon managing media pressure during incidents [48] and the challenges of involving private forest owners [49].

source_name: Forest Fire Fighting Guidance - 3rd Edition 2022
topic: Forest fire control, tactical guidance, and operational procedures
summary: This is the 3rd edition of the 'Forest Fire Fighting Guidance', published in July 2022 by the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency (MSB) [61, 62]. Primarily aimed at municipal rescue services personnel, its purpose is to strengthen knowledge about fire behavior, especially in extreme conditions, and provide knowledge transfer from previous forest fires [62, 63]. The guidance covers topics such as forest fire detection in Sweden, assessing fire spread and extent, including the influence of wind and the Fire Behavior Prediction (FBP) model [64, 65]. It also includes sections on requesting airborne support (helicopters and water bombing aircraft), piloting multiple aircraft, and environmental considerations [66]. The document emphasizes the importance of situation monitoring and documentation using GIS analyses and the SiTaC system, particularly after large incidents where information can be scattered [67, 68].

source_name: National Aerial Firefighting Strategy 2021-26
topic: National aerial firefighting strategy, capability, and needs
summary: This document outlines the National Aerial Firefighting Strategy for 2021–26, published in June 2021 [69]. It covers the strategic intent, risk management, current aerial firefighting capability, and future needs [69]. The document also includes image credits from Australian fire services like the Country Fire Authority and NSW Rural Fire Service, indicating its regional focus [69].

source_name: The NIST Wildland-Urban Interface Fire Case Study Approach and Outlook
topic: Wildland-urban interface (WUI) fire case study methodology, data collection, and research outlook
summary: This NIST Technical Note, published in July 2024, describes 'The NIST Wildland-Urban Interface Fire Case Study Approach and Outlook' [70, 71]. It summarizes four past in-depth case studies conducted since 2007, which have served as a technical anchor for NIST's WUI research [71, 72]. The document details the methodology for data collection and analysis, including the use of WUI 0, WUI 1, and WUI 2 levels of complexity [73, 74]. Data collection involves methodical documentation of structure construction, ignition locations, damage levels, fuels, fire spread indicators, and exposure sources, preferring a mobile GIS application for data entry [75]. Key technical themes for data collection include spatiotemporal fire progression, weather, topography, wildland environment, response of structures and communities, human response, and emergency response [76]. The report emphasizes the need for continued in-depth case studies to inform scientific advancement, confirm mitigation efficacy, and identify improvements for community resilience and first responder safety [77, 78]. It also suggests maintaining connections with states across different U.S. regions to study diverse fuels, topographies, and construction practices [79].

filename: NSW & ACT Aviation Standard Operating Procedures 2018 V4.1.pdf
source_name: NSW & ACT Aviation Standard Operating Procedures 2018
topic: Aviation Standard Operating Procedures for fire services
region: New South Wales & Australian Capital Territory, Australia
summary: This document contains the 'NSW & ACT Aviation Standard Operating Procedures 2018 V4.1', originally developed by the NSW Rural Fire Service [80]. It acknowledges input from various agencies including Fire and Rescue NSW, National Parks and Wildlife Service, ACT Rural Fire Service, and others [80]. The material is copyrighted by the State of New South Wales through the NSW Rural Fire Service, encouraging free use for personal, in-house, or non-commercial purposes with proper attribution [80].

source_name: Portugal Aerial Firefighting Main Report
topic: Strategic analysis of Portugal's aerial fire management capacity
summary: This main report details a strategic analysis project established to review Portugal's aerial fire management capacity, with a focus on capabilities required beyond 2025 [81]. The project was sponsored by the Autoridade Nacional de Emergência e Proteção Civil (Civil Protection Authority, ANEPC) and the Força Aérea Portuguesa (Portuguese Air Force, FAP) [82]. It identifies key characteristics of Portugal's environment important for aerial fire management [83]. The report suggests that the main agencies involved in aerial firefighting collaborate to produce and publish a 'National Aerial Firefighting Strategic Plan' to summarize governance, responsibilities, and guiding principles [84, 85]. It also addresses operational and technical issues identified during the project [86, 87], including the use of various extinguishing agents like water, foam, and retardants [88].

source_name: Rapid Aerial Fire Fighting Teams
topic: Rapid Aerial Fire Fighting Teams operational procedures
summary: This document, approved in August 2022, pertains to 'Rapid Aerial Fire Fighting Teams' (RART) [89]. It references 'RART Activation Triggers' as an appendix and lists 'Interagency Aviation SOPs 2018' as a related document [89].

source_name: Interagency Standards for Fire and Fire Aviation Operations (Red Book)
topic: Interagency standards for fire and fire aviation operations in the U.S. federal agencies
summary: This document, titled 'Interagency Standards for Fire and Fire Aviation Operations' and known as the 'Red Book', is produced by the Interagency Standards for Fire and Fire Aviation Operations Group at the National Interagency Fire Center in Boise, ID, with a release date of January 2025 [90]. It provides guidance for implementing safe and effective fire and aviation management operations for various U.S. federal agencies, including the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), U.S. Forest Service (USFS), U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), National Park Service (NPS), and Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) [91-96]. The document addresses specific action items from the 'Guidance for Implementation of Federal Wildland Fire Management Policy' [97]. It covers a wide range of topics, including program organization and responsibilities for each agency [94-96, 98, 99], fire planning and fuels management [100-103], preparedness reviews [104-107], incident management and response using the Wildland Fire Decision Support System (WFDSS) [108, 109], firefighting equipment [110-112], suppression chemicals [113], reviews and investigations [114], and dispatch and coordination systems [115]. The Red Book emphasizes safety, collaboration, and adherence to interagency standards for all wildland fire activities [92, 104, 116].

filename: Reporting fire in Australia’s forests and vegetation.pdf
source_name: Reporting Fire in Australia’s Forests and Vegetation
topic: Reporting and monitoring fire in Australian forests and vegetation, data quality, and national databases
summary: This report, titled 'Reporting Fire in Australia’s Forests and Vegetation', assesses the quality, completeness, and availability of fire information to enable reporting on the Montreal Process indicator 3.1, which focuses on forest health and vitality affected by processes beyond historic variation [117, 118]. It highlights that a coordinated and standardized national approach is needed for gathering accurate fire data, including intensity and damage indices, as no single State or Territory agency can currently provide comprehensive, up-to-date analysis nationally [118]. The report details fire incident reporting, data collection, and datasets across various Australian states and territories, including Tasmania, New South Wales, South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland, and the Northern Territory, noting the varying levels of detail and accuracy in recording information like vegetation type burnt and fire severity [119-131]. It discusses the reliance on satellite data for remote areas and the challenges of capturing small, low-intensity fires [132]. The authors suggest that significant resources are needed to collate existing data and develop models for fire intensity and severity to achieve meaningful national reporting [133, 134].

source_name: Summary Inspector-General Emergency Management Queensland Bushfire Review Report 2: 2019-20
topic: Queensland bushfire review, community insights, and disaster management
summary: This document provides a summary of the 'Inspector-General Emergency Management Queensland Bushfire Review Report 2: 2019-20', focusing on observations, insights, and case studies from the September 2019 bushfire events in Queensland, Australia [135, 136]. The review aimed to maximize community safety outcomes and provide independent assurance to the Queensland Government [136]. Key findings include that bushfire was identified as the most likely disaster type to occur in all three regions surveyed, and while respondents knew lead organizations like QFES, few identified the Local Disaster Management Group (LDMG) as having a role, indicating an opportunity to build LDMG awareness [137]. The report emphasizes community engagement and applied research for fire management, fire ecology, and biodiversity conservation in Queensland [138].

source_name: Technical Recommendation: Aerial Firefighting Air Operations for and by the fire service
topic: Aerial firefighting air operations and tactical guidelines for fire services
summary: This document, a technical recommendation from the German Fire Service Association, provides guidelines for 'Aircraft Operations / Aerial Firefighting Air Operations for and by the fire service' [139, 140]. Developed from a workshop and based on international training literature and experiences from countries with long-standing wildfire experience like France, Spain, and the USA [141, 142]. The recommendation addresses the increasing use of aircraft in firefighting due to frequent dry periods in Central Europe [139, 141]. It covers tactical framework conditions, technical possibilities for aircraft operations in Germany, safe cooperation between air and ground forces, command and control, extinguishing agents, and pilot/aircrew training [143, 144]. It also notes the difference between ICAO categories for extinguishing agent provision at landing sites and helicopter classification typically used in international aerial firefighting [145].

source_name: The National Strategy: The Final Phase in the Development of the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy
topic: National cohesive wildland fire management strategy for the United States
summary: This report, 'The National Strategy', is the culmination of a three-phased, intergovernmental planning and analysis process for a national cohesive wildland fire management strategy in the United States, as mandated by the Federal Land Assistance, Management, and Enhancement (FLAME) Act of 2009 [146-148]. It outlines three primary goals: restore and maintain landscapes, create fire-adapted communities, and improve wildfire response [147]. The strategy addresses national challenges, categorized into vegetation and fuels, homes/communities and other values at risk, human-caused ignitions, and effective and efficient wildfire response [149-152]. It includes regional characterizations for the Northeast, Southeast, and West, detailing diverse ecosystems, land ownership patterns, fire season characteristics, and factors influencing wildfire threats [153-155]. The document emphasizes the importance of collaboration among federal, state, local, and tribal governments and non-governmental partners [146, 156, 157], and how data analysis and spatially explicit priorities can inform efforts such as grant funding for wildfire risk mitigation [158].

filename: Thirtymile Fire Investigation Accident Investigation Factual Report and Management Evaluation Report.pdf
source_name: Thirtymile Fire Investigation Accident Investigation Factual Report and Management Evaluation Report
topic: Investigation of the Thirtymile Fire accident, including fire behavior, human factors, and equipment
summary: This document is the 'Thirtymile Fire Investigation Accident Investigation Factual Report and Management Evaluation Report', providing a detailed overview of the Thirtymile Fire incident [159]. It describes the initial actions, the roles of different crews like the Northwest Regulars #6 and Entiat IHC, air support, and engines, leading up to the entrapment and deployment of firefighters [159]. The report includes extensive appendices covering critical aspects such as fire behavior, weather conditions, human factors like fatigue levels of key personnel, equipment used, and the qualifications of the firefighters involved [160-164]. It also emphasizes lessons learned regarding fire shelter training and the need to secure packs away from deployment areas [165].

filename: Vegetation Fire Fighting Training Manual for Fire Departments Version 1.pdf
source_name: Vegetation Fire Fighting Training Manual for Fire Departments Version 1
topic: Vegetation fire fighting training manual for fire departments, covering safety, equipment, tactics, and ecological aspects
summary: This 'Vegetation Fire Fighting Training Manual for Fire Departments Version 1', dated December 2024, aims to comprehensively prepare firefighters for the complex challenges of vegetation firefighting, with a clear focus on the safety of emergency responders [166-168]. It covers various aspects of vegetation firefighting, including a hazard matrix, descriptions of equipment for different operational scenarios [167], and logistics for staging areas and mobile supply units [169]. The manual emphasizes the importance of early fire detection through technological systems like thermal sensors and satellite-based monitoring [170]. It also integrates ecological aspects, such as the benefits of structurally rich forests for biodiversity and resilience to environmental changes, advocating for differentiated deadwood management and targeted silvicultural measures to minimize fire risk [170-172]. The manual also stresses the need for continuous training and practice [173], and highlights the reliance on a robust database and scientific findings for fire assessment [174].

source_name: Vegetation Fire Fighting: Basics
topic: Basic principles and tactics for vegetation fire fighting
summary: This document, 'Vegetation Fire Fighting: Basics', serves as a foundational guide for firefighting operations [175, 176]. It covers essential topics such as equipment for a group, safety rules, locating emergency sites in unmarked areas, firefighting with fire engines, water extraction points, and various vegetation fire fighting tactics including direct fire attack and creating and securing firebreaks [175, 176]. The guide is structured to provide fundamental understanding and practical advice for self-sufficient firefighting teams [176].

source_name: A comprehensive Swedish database for forest and land fires
topic: Need for and design of a comprehensive national database for forest and land fires in Sweden
summary: This report, 'A comprehensive Swedish database for forest and land fires', published in 2023, explores the need for a national database for wildfires and management fires in Sweden [177-179]. It highlights that despite discussions over the past 20 years, such a comprehensive database does not yet exist, hindering fire protection and nature conservation efforts [179, 180]. The report details what basic information should be collected for each fire, including coordinates for the starting point and a shape-file delineating the perimeter, cause, weather, and fire risk index [181-186]. It discusses current data collection methods by rescue services, MSB, Swedish Forest Agency, and satellite monitoring [187-189]. The document emphasizes the importance of linking weather and fire danger indices to each fire to enhance the database's utility for long-term biomonitoring and wildfire risk assessments, especially in the context of climate change [182, 186]. It concludes by recommending a meeting between key Swedish agencies to agree on cooperation and structure information collection [190].

source_name: NWCG Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG)
topic: Wildland fire incident response guidance, safety, and operational procedures
summary: The 'NWCG Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG)', published by the National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) in January 2022, serves as a key reference for wildland firefighters [191, 192]. It is designed to assist in reporting critical information upon arrival at an incident, including incident type, location, size, status, and resource needs [191]. The guide emphasizes the importance of competent and confident leadership in wildland firefighting, which involves providing purpose, direction, and motivation in dangerous and stressful situations [193]. It covers operational leadership, guidelines for long-term incidents, fire origin protection, and communication [194-196]. The IRPG also provides detailed sections on various strategies and tactics, such as direct and indirect attack, fireline location, use of heavy equipment, water delivery, and aerial firefighting considerations like directing retardant and bucket drops, and aircraft mishap response actions [197]. The document is available electronically and in print from the Great Basin Cache at the National Interagency Fire Center [192].
